intro: This branch builds multiplication from equal groups, through the times tables, to multiplying large numbers on paper. Multiplication is a fast way to add equal groups, and it underpins division, fractions and area.

II.2.01.what: Seeing multiplication as a number of equal groups, such as 3 groups of 2.

levels.a: Counts groups of 2 and finds how many there are in all.
levels.b: Finds the total for groups of 5 and groups of 10.
levels.c: Writes equal groups as a repeated addition, like 8 + 8.
levels.d: Rewrites a repeated addition as a multiplication, like 2 times 8.

II.2.02.what: Using arrays (objects set out in neat rows and columns) to picture multiplication.

levels.a: Counts the rows and columns in an array.
levels.b: Writes the multiplication that an array shows.
levels.c: Sees that turning an array on its side gives the same total, so 8 times 3 equals 3 times 8.
levels.d: Plans an array to show a given multiplication fact.

II.2.03.what: Learning the easiest times tables first: multiplying by 0, 1, 2, 5 and 10.

levels.a: Knows that times 0 gives 0 and times 1 leaves a number unchanged.

levels.b: Finds 4 times a number by doubling it, then doubling again.
levels.d: Answers a mix of 3, 4 and 6 times table facts.

II.2.05.what: Learning the harder 7, 8 and 9 times tables.

levels.a: Uses patterns in the 9 times table to find facts.
levels.d: Answers a mix of 7, 8 and 9 times table facts.

II.2.06.what: Bringing all the times tables up to 10 times 10 together until they are quick and reliable.

levels.a: Knows the square facts, where a number is multiplied by itself, like 7 times 7.
levels.b: Works out a new fact from one already known, such as doubling 4 times 8 to get 8 times 8.
levels.c: Answers a mix of facts from across all the tables.
levels.d: Recalls any fact from memory, including finding a missing number.

II.2.07.what: Picturing multiplication as the area of a rectangle, which later explains how to multiply bigger numbers.

levels.a: Counts the unit squares that cover a rectangle.
levels.b: Finds the area by multiplying length by width.
levels.c: Splits a rectangle into two parts and adds their areas.
levels.d: Splits a multiplication the same way, as in 3 times 18 = 3 times 10 plus 3 times 8.

II.2.08.what: Learning the rules multiplication always follows, which make calculations easier.

levels.a: Knows the order doesn't matter: 4 times 7 equals 7 times 4.
levels.b: Knows grouping doesn't matter when multiplying three numbers.
levels.c: Splits a number to multiply in parts, as in 3 times 18 = 3 times 10 plus 3 times 8.
levels.d: Uses these rules to make a calculation easy, like 2 times 16 times 5.
levels.e: Regroups a product like 25 times 83 times 4 to make it easy (25 times 4 is 100).
levels.f: Spots a shared number in two products and combines them, as in 7 times 37 plus 3 times 37.

II.2.09.what: Multiplying by 10, 100, 1,000 and numbers like 40 or 300 using known facts and zeros.

levels.b: Multiplies a one-digit number by a multiple of ten, like 3 times 80.
levels.c: Multiplies two multiples of ten, like 30 times 80.

II.2.10.what: Multiplying a two-digit number by a one-digit number, such as 28 times 8.

levels.a: Uses a split rectangle (area model) to multiply tens and ones separately.
levels.b: Writes the tens and ones products separately, then adds them.
levels.c: Uses the standard written method with carrying.
levels.d: Estimates first by rounding, then finds the exact answer.

II.2.11.what: Multiplying a three- or four-digit number by a one-digit number.

levels.a: Multiplies each place separately, then adds the parts.
levels.b: Handles the carrying from one column to the next.
levels.c: Uses the standard written method from start to finish.
levels.d: Estimates to pick out the correct answer.

II.2.12.what: Multiplying two two-digit numbers, such as 28 times 86.

levels.a: Uses a rectangle split into four parts to find the product.
levels.b: Writes the four partial products, then adds them.
levels.c: Finishes the standard written method with two rows.
levels.d: Estimates by rounding both numbers, then finds the exact answer.
levels.e: Finds a missing digit in a two-digit multiplication.
levels.f: Arranges four digit cards into two numbers that make the largest possible product.

II.2.13.what: Multiplying bigger numbers, such as a three-digit number by a two-digit number.

levels.a: Multiplies a three-digit number by a two-digit number.
levels.b: Does the same when zeros appear in the numbers.
levels.c: Works through the written method row by row with confidence.
levels.d: Picks out which answer is reasonable by estimating.

II.2.14.what: Using multiplication to solve everyday word problems.

levels.a: Solves problems about equal groups, like vases holding the same number of flowers.
levels.b: Solves problems about rows and columns, like tiles on a wall.
levels.c: Solves problems saying one thing is some number of times as much as another.
levels.d: Solves problems that take more than one step.
levels.e: Works backwards: undoes a chain of steps to find the number someone started with.
levels.f: Solves classic puzzles like 'chickens and cows: 26 heads, 78 legs; how many chickens?'

II.2.15.what: Spotting and explaining patterns in multiplication.

levels.a: Recognizes which numbers belong to a given times table.
levels.b: Tells whether a product will be even or odd without multiplying.
levels.c: Makes a product easier by halving one number and doubling the other.
levels.d: Explains why a pattern happens, such as why doubling one number doubles the answer.
levels.e: Finds the last digit of a big product using only the last digits.
levels.f: Finds the last digit of a number multiplied by itself many times, using a repeating cycle.
